 1                                      PRELIMINARY STATEMENT

 2            1.      This is a proposed class action seeking monetary damages, restitution, and injunctive

 3 and declaratory relief from Defendant FTD, LLC arising from its use of deceptive addition of hidden
 4 fees which unfairly inflates the prices of floral deliveries over and above the advertised prices.
 5            2.      When consumers purchase flowers for delivery through FTD’s website, FTD

 6 prominently advertises pricing that is drastically altered by the time the payment screen populates.
 7 On the payment screen consumers are surprised with surreptitiously added “Delivery Fee”
 8 (collectively “Fees”) to their online floral delivery.
 9            3.      As discussed in detail herein, the assessment of these Fees is deceptive and unfair,

10 since, a) FTD advertised one price for floral deliveries, only to later disclose a higher, different price
11 later in the checkout process; and b) the Fees are in actuality simply the price of ordering flowers for
12 delivery.
13            4.      At various stages of the ordering process, FTD’s website asks consumers to input their

14 delivery details (i.e., delivery zip code and date) to show available products and pricing. Despite this,
15 throughout the entirety of the ordering process, FTD displays a single price for floral delivery, up
16 until the very last step. The last-minute addition of the “Delivery Fee” renders FTD’s advertised
17 pricing false and a classic bait-and-switch. Obscuring the total price to lure in consumers is deceptive
18 and unfair because it “interferes with consumers’ ability to price-compare and manipulates them into
19 paying fees that are either hidden entirely or not presented until late in the transaction, after the
20 consumer already has spent significant time selecting and finalizing a product or service plan to
21 purchase.”1
22            5.      FTD misrepresents the actual costs of purchasing floral deliveries to consumers.

23            6.      Hundreds of thousands of FTD customers like Plaintiff have been assessed hidden fees

24 for which they did not bargain.
25            7.      Consumers like Plaintiff reasonably understand FTD’s advertised price to disclose the

 4           9.     Plaintiff brings her claims individually and on behalf of all similarly situated

 5 consumers who have been misled by FTD’s advertisements and seeks monetary damages and, among

 7 at the start of the purchase process.
 8                                                 PARTIES

 9           10.    Plaintiff Taylor Pulbrook is a resident and a citizen of San Jose, California.

10           11.    Defendant FTD, LLC is an online floral delivery company headquartered in Chicago,

11 Illinois.
12                                     JURISDICTION AND VENUE

13           12.    This Court has original jurisdiction over this action under the Class Action Fairness

14 Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1332(d)(2). The amount in controversy exceeds $5 million, exclusive of interest and
15 costs, there are more than 100 members in the proposed class, and at least one member of the class is
16 a citizen of a state different from Defendant, including Plaintiff.
17           13.    This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendant because Defendant does

18 substantial business in California.
19           14.    Venue is proper in this Court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b) because a substantial

20 part of the events, acts, and omissions giving rise to Plaintiff’s claims occurred in this District.
21                   FACTUAL BACKGROUND AND GENERAL ALLEGATIONS

22           A.     FTD’s Website Fails to Bind Users to Any Terms of Service

23           15.    When a consumer selects an item for purchase on the FTD website, she then enters

24 into a multi-step purchasing process in which she is shown screens that, in order: 1) show her
25 shopping cart reflecting a subtotal (without the added delivery fees or applicable tax) and require
26 entry of contact and delivery information; and (2) require entry of payment information.
27           16.    During the multi-step checkout process, FTD users are never provided with FTD’s

28 terms of service; are never required to view such terms of service; and are never required to

 2          17.     Additionally, FTD fails to hyperlink its Terms of Service on any of the mentioned

 3 screens shown to users.

 5          18.     FTD, LLC is one of the largest online flower and gift delivery retailers in the world. It

 6 operates a website, FTD.com, which allow consumers to send flowers or gifts for delivery.
 7          19.     On the homepage and each product page, consumers are prompted to search for

 1          28.     FTD strategically buried their delivery price in a hyperlink at the bottom of the page

 2 and in small font to conceal this material information from its users and misrepresent the true cost of
 3 ordering from its website.
 4          29.     Reasonable consumers are not expected to ferret out material information, such as

 5 mandatory fees or the true price of a product or service, by scouring every hyperlink on a website.
 6          30.     By assessing “Delivery Fees” to all floral arrangement orders placed on FTD’s

 7 website, the advertised price for any specific floral arrangement for delivery is false.
 8          31.     By unfairly obscuring the true price to consumers, FTD deceives consumers and gains

 9 an unfair upper hand on competitors that fairly and transparently disclose their mandatory fees.
10 Indeed, other major online flower delivery providers in the U.S. do not assess fees outside of those
11 properly disclosed at the outset of a consumer’s order.
12          30.     In short, the disclosed item cost on FTD’s website is not accurate. The actual cost for

13 flower delivery is the listed subtotal plus the “Delivery Fee” that FTD deceptively adds late in the
14 ordering process.
15          31.     FTD does not inform consumers the true costs of its floral delivery service and it

16 misrepresents the price of any given floral delivery, when in fact those costs are actually higher.
17          32.     Moreover, the additional fees assessed are never reasonably disclosed to consumers

18 until it shows up on the final page of checkout as a line item in their order summary—after the
19 purchase process is largely complete. This process fails to provide an adequate advance warning to
20 customers that additional, mandatory fees will be imposed on their purchases.
21          33.     Many consumers do not notice these fees are being added to their order. And others

22 still notice the previously undisclosed fees but decide to go through with the purchase anyway because
23 they have already invested substantial time and effort inputting their information into the FTD’s
24 system. So it doesn’t make sense to start over and research whether there is a way to avoid these fees.
25 The deceptive checkout practice has done its job and diverted the sale to FTD.
26          34.     Further, because Defendant waited until the end of the checkout process to disclose

27 the true price, it is difficult for consumers to accurately compare floral delivery prices across other
28 online flower delivery providers. Not only does this frustrate comparison shopping, but this drip

 1 pricing also impeded competition and led consumers to pay more for their floral deliveries than they
 2 otherwise would have.
 3          35.     This is a classic case of “Drip pricing”. “Drip pricing” works because as research has

 4 shown, “our brains tend to fix on the price we first encountered even after we learn the total cost. And
 5 even when consumers learn about the hidden fees, they often pay up rather than shop around . . .
 6 because they figure that ‘investing more time into searching for it will not be worthwhile.’”2
 7          36.     By unfairly obscuring its delivery charges to consumers, FTD deceives consumers and

 8 gains an unfair upper hand on competitors that fairly disclose their true charges.
 9          D.      The Delivery Fees Are Junk Fees That Violate Federal Guidance

10          37.     FTD’s fees are precisely the type of “Junk Fees” that has come under government

11 scrutiny in recent years:
12          Junk fees are fees that are mandatory but not transparently disclosed to consumers.
            Consumers are lured in with the promise of a low price, but when they get to the
13          register, they discover that price was never really available. Junk fees harm consumers
            and actively undermine competition by making it impractical for consumers to
14          compare prices, a linchpin of our economic system.
15

 1          39.     In July of 2024, California amended its Consumer Legal Remedies Act (“CLRA”) to

 2 make illegal “drip pricing,” which involves advertising a price that is less than the actual price that a
 3 consumer will have to pay for a good or service. California Civil Code Section 1770(a)(29). Under
 4 the new California law, it is now illegal to advertise a low price for a product, only for that product
 5 to be subject to additional or mandatory fees later. In other words, “the price listed or advertised to
 6 the consumer must be the full price that the consumer is required to pay.” See California Department
 7 of Justice, Office of the Attorney General, SB 478 Frequently Asked Questions, available at
 8 https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/attachments/press-docs/SB%20478%20FAQ%20%28B%29.pdf (last
 9 accessed July 18, 2024). As the California Department of Justice stated:
10          Businesses are free to explain how they set their prices or to subsequently itemize the
            charges that make up the total price that they charge customers. However, the price
11          they advertise or display must be the total price that customers will have to pay for the
            good or service. Knowing the price of a good of service is essential to competition,
12          and displaying a price that is less than what the customer will actually be charged is
            deceptive.
13
14 Id. at p. 4 (emphasis added).
15          40.     In its 2013 publication “.com Disclosures: How to Make Effective Disclosures in

16 Digital Advertising, the FTC makes clear that when advertising and selling are combined on a
17 website, and the consumer will be completing the transaction online, the disclosures should be
18 provided before the consumer makes the decision to buy – for example, before the consumer “add[s]
19 to shopping cart.” See Fed. Trade Comm’n, How to Make Effective Disclosures in Digital Advertising
20 at ii, 14 (Mar. 2013), available at https://www.ftc.gov/sites/default/files/attachments/press-
21 releases/ftc-staff-revises-online-advertising-disclosure-guidelines/130312dotcomdisclosures.pdf.
22          41.     Defendant violates federal guidance by adding the “Delivery Fees” as a line item well

23 after the consumer “add[s] to shopping cart”, and by failing to disclose the nature of these fees and
24 whether consumers are getting any benefit at all from the fee charged.
25          E.      Plaintiff Pulbrook’s Experience

26          42.     Plaintiff Pulbrook used the FTD website to place a floral arrangement delivery order

27 on January 24, 2025.
28          43.     When using the website, Plaintiff was repeatedly informed that her floral delivery cart

26           50.    Commonality: There are questions of law or fact common to the Class, which

27 include, but are not limited to the following:

 8          64.     Defendant’s conduct described herein violates the Unfair Competition Law (“UCL”),

 9 codified at California Business and Professions Code section 17200, et seq.
10          65.     The UCL prohibits, and provides civil remedies for, unfair competition. Its purpose is

11 to protect both consumers and competitors by promoting fair competition in commercial markets for
12 goods and services. In service of that purpose, the Legislature framed the UCL’s substantive
13 provisions in broad, sweeping language.
14          66.     The UCL imposes strict liability. Plaintiff need not prove that Defendant intentionally

15 or negligently engaged in unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business practices—but only that such
16 practices occurred.
17          67.     A business act or practice is “unfair” under the UCL if it offends an established public

18 policy or is immoral, unethical, oppressive, unscrupulous, or substantially injurious to consumers,
19 and that unfairness is determined by weighing the reasons, justifications, and motives of the practice
20 against the gravity of the harm to the alleged victims.
21          68.     A business act or practice is “fraudulent” under the UCL if it is likely to deceive

22 members of the public.
23          69.     A business act or practice is “unlawful” under the UCL if it violates any other law or

24 regulation.
25          70.     Defendant committed unfair and fraudulent business acts and practices in violation of

26 Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200, et seq., by affirmatively and knowingly misrepresenting that the
27 presence and nature of its Delivery Fees.
28          71.     Defendant’s acts and practices offend an established public policy of truthful

                                                     COMPLETING THE CIVIL COVER SHEET
Complete the form as follows:
 I.   Plaintiffs-Defendants. Enter names (last, first, middle initial) of plaintiff and defendant. If the plaintiff or defendant is a government agency, use the
      full name or standard abbreviations. If the plaintiff or defendant is an official within a government agency, identify first the agency and then the
      official, giving both name and title.
      County of Residence. For each civil case filed, except U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county where the first listed plaintiff resides at the
      time of filing. In U.S. plaintiff cases, enter the name of the county in which the first listed defendant resides at the time of filing. In land
      condemnation cases, the county of residence of the “defendant” is the location of the tract of land involved.
      Attorney/Pro Se Litigant Information. Enter the firm name, address, telephone number, and email for attorney of record or pro se litigant. If there
      are several individuals, list them on an attachment.

 II. Jurisdiction. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 8(a), pleadings must establish the basis of jurisdiction. If multiple bases for jurisdiction apply,
     prioritize them in the order listed:
      (1) United States plaintiff. Jurisdiction based on 28 U.S.C. §§ 1345 and 1348 for suits filed by the United States, its agencies or officers.
      (2) United States defendant. Applies when the United States, its agencies, or officers are defendants.
      (3) Federal question. Select this option when jurisdiction is based on 28 U.S.C. § 1331 for cases involving the U.S. Constitution, its amendments,
          federal laws, or treaties (but use choices 1 or 2 if the United States is a party).
       (4) Diversity of citizenship. Select this option when jurisdiction is based on 28 U.S.C. § 1332 for cases between citizens of different states and
           complete Section VI to specify the parties’ citizenship. Note: Federal question jurisdiction takes precedence over diversity jurisdiction.
 III. Cause of Action. Enter the statute directly related to the cause of action and give a brief description of the cause. Do not cite jurisdictional statutes
      unless jurisdiction is based on diversity. Example: U.S. Civil Statute: 47 U.S.C. § 553. Brief Description: Unauthorized reception of cable service.
 IV. Nature of Suit. Check one of the boxes. If the case fits more than one nature of suit, select the most definitive or predominant.
 V.   Origin. Check one of the boxes:
      (1) Original Proceedings. Cases originating in the United States district courts.
      (2) Removed from State Court. Proceedings initiated in state courts may be removed to the district courts under Title 28 U.S.C. § 1441. When the
          petition for removal is granted, check this box.
      (3) Remanded from Appellate Court. Check this box for cases remanded to the district court for further action, using the date of remand as the
          filing date.
      (4) Reinstated or Reopened. Check this box for cases reinstated or reopened in the district court. Use the reopening date as the filing date.
      (5) Transferred from Another District. Check this box for cases transferred under Title 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). Do not use this for within-district
          transfers or multidistrict litigation (MDL) transfers.
      (6) Multidistrict Litigation Transfer. Check this box when a multidistrict (MDL) case is transferred into the district under authority of Title 28
          U.S.C. § 1407.
      (7) Multidistrict Litigation Direct File. Check this box when a multidistrict litigation case is filed in the same district as the Master MDL docket.
 VI. Residence (citizenship) of Principal Parties. Mark for each principal party only if jurisdiction is based on diversity of citizenship.
 VII. Requested in Complaint.
      (1) Jury demand. Check this box if plaintiff's complaint demanded a jury trial.
      (2) Monetary demand. For cases demanding monetary relief, check this box and enter the actual dollar amount being demanded.
      (3) Class action. Check this box if plaintiff is filing a class action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 23.
      (4) Nationwide injunction. Check this box if plaintiff is seeking a nationwide injunction or nationwide vacatur pursuant to the Administrative
          Procedures Act.
 VIII.   Related Cases. If there are related pending case(s), provide the case name(s) and number(s) and the name(s) of the presiding judge(s). If a short-
     form MDL complaint is being filed, furnish the MDL case name and number.
 IX. Divisional Assignment. Identify the divisional venue according to Civil Local Rule 3-2: “the county in which a substantial part of the events or
     omissions which give rise to the claim occurred or in which a substantial part of the property that is the subject of the action is situated.” Note that
     case assignment is made without regard for division in the following case types: Property Rights (Patent, Trademark and Copyright), Prisoner
     Petitions, Securities Class Actions, Anti-Trust, Bankruptcy, Social Security, and Tax.
